title: any, anywhere, many
parentNote: Any and many are the same lie told twice: the a in the middle of each one says e. Any is enny and many is menny, and there is nothing on the page that says so. Say them as a pair, one after the other, because a child who has learned one has very nearly learned the other. Then anywhere, which is different in a way worth pointing at: it is not a new word at all, it is any and where — a word from today and a word from four days ago — pushed together. Show them the join. Cover the last five letters, read any; slide your hand along, read where; then read the whole thing. That trick works on hundreds of long words later on and this is a good one to learn it on. What these three actually buy you is the ability to talk about nothing and about lots: not any left, so many bugs, it could be anywhere. Those are things a child says fifty times a day and has not until now been able to read.

activities.sentence: Are there any plums left on the tree?
activities.prompt: Do not sound this out. That a in the middle is saying e, so the word is enny. Any.

activities.sentence: There are so many bugs on this plant.
activities.prompt: Exactly the same trick. The a says e again, so this one is menny. Any, many. Two words, one lie.
This is the sound in the middle of any and many, even though the letter sitting there is an a. Find the letter that really makes this sound.
Two of these you just know and one of them you can sound out. Listen right to the end of each.

activities.sentence: My red sock is not anywhere in the shed.
activities.prompt: This is a long one, and it is not new. Cover the end and read any. Cover the front and read where. Now push them together: anywhere.
One of these is the other two stuck together. Listen for the long one.
No new sound today. All of these you can sound out, and all of them are in the story at the end.
The long one. Five sounds. Take the first three, then the last two, then put the halves together.
All three start with pl. Everything you need is the sound in the middle.
This one is hard. All three start with tr and all three end with a long sound. Listen to that last sound.

activities.text: Are there any buns left, or did Meg eat all of them?
There are so many bugs on this plant that I can not see the plant.
You can sit anywhere you want, but you can not sit here.
I did hunt for my red sock all morning, and it is not anywhere in the shed.

activities.title: So many plums
activities.prompt: This story starts with far too many and ends with not any. See if you can spot the bit where it tips.
lines: There is a plum tree at the end of the yard, and this week it is thick with plums.
"Do we want any?" said Meg. "We want all of them," I said.
So we did get a big tin and we did pick plums all morning.
Meg did pick the plums she can get to, and I did get up on a box for the rest.
We did fill the tin. Then we did fill a jar. Then we did fill the hat that Dad did lend us.
"That is so many plums," said Meg. "I do not think we can eat this many."
We did eat plums with lunch. We did eat plums on the step. By six we did not want any more.
Meg did go a bit green and did sit down on the grass with a thud.
So Mum did get the big pot out, and all of the plums did go in it, and now there is jam.
There is jam in the shed, jam on the shelf and jam under the sink. There is not anywhere left to keep it.
Then we did go and check the tree. There are not any plums on it at all.
Not a plum anywhere. We did get the lot, and now we do not want any.
Mum did hand me a bun. "Do you want jam on it?" she said. For the first time, I said no.
